articleOfWeek.title: Measurement properties of pulmonary function measurement and patient-reported outcome measures in patients with multiple rib fracture without flail segment; validation study alongside the multicenter FixCon trial.
articleOfWeek.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articleOfWeek.abstract: The reliability and validity of pulmonary function, pain and health related quality of life (HR-QoL) as outcome measures for patients with rib fractures, remain uncertain. Our objective was to evaluate measurement properties in patients with multiple rib fractures by comparing them with generic HR-QoL instruments (EuroQoL-5D-5L [EQ-5D-5L], Short Form-12 [SF-12]). A multicenter RCT in adults (n = 180) was performed. Spirometry was performed at 30 days, 3, 6, and 12 months after trauma. Patients completed five questions on pain, EQ-5D-5L, SF-12, and two anchor questions on improvement in pulmonary function and thoracic complaints since previous measurement. Reliability, construct validity, responsiveness and floor and ceiling effects were evaluated for all follow-up time-points. EQ-5D and SF-12 (sub)scales showed adequate internal consistency. Construct and longitudinal validity were adequate for all (sub)scales, except for construct validity of the SF-12 Physical Component Summary. Ceiling effects were present for all pain questions from 30 days onwards, for EQ-5D-5L utility score (US) from 3 months onwards. Responsiveness analysis indicated that spirometry values showed trivial (tidal volume), small (inspiratory capacity, FEV1), or moderate (FVC) degree of change from 30 days to 12 months. All five pain levels, EQ-5D-5L and SF-12 (sub)scales showed moderate to large degree of change form 30 days to 12 months. Spirometry and pain are valid instruments for monitoring functional recovery in patients after sustaining multiple rib fractures. Responsiveness was confirmed for pain and spirometry (FVC). EQ-5D-5L and SF-12 are valid, reliable, and responsive. Pain and HRQoL are therefore suitable instruments for measuring treatment effects over time.

articles.title: Irisin is associated with survival in sepsis and attenuates macrophage pro-inflammatory responses with involvement of AMPK signaling.
articles.abstract: Sepsis is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality, yet effective targeted therapies remain limited. We evaluated the prognostic significance of irisin, a myokine, in sepsis cohort and examined its immunomodulatory effects on macrophages using a translational approach. Patients were enrolled in a prospectively collected sepsis registry and biobank. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards model was conducted to assess independent association between irisin and 30-day mortality. Mechanistic studies used macrophages ex vivo and a murine cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) model. Higher serum irisin was independently associated with lower 30-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 0.955, 95% confidence interval 0.913-0.999, p=0.044) in patients with sepsis (N=655). Irisin showed modest discrimination for 30-day mortality (AUROC 0.609), with no statistically significant difference from lactate (AUROC 0.652; p=0.145). In vitro, irisin suppressed LPS-induced pro-inflammatory cytokine production, preserved AMPK phosphorylation, attenuated IκBα degradation, and reduced pro-inflammatory markers in macrophages. Several of these cellular effects were attenuated following AMPKα1 depletion. In vivo, irisin improved 7-day survival after CLP (75% vs. 36%, p<0.05) and reduced systemic inflammatory cytokines at 24 hours. Higher serum irisin was independently associated with lower 30-day mortality in patients with sepsis, although its standalone discriminatory performance was modest. Experimental findings further showed that irisin improved survival and attenuated macrophage inflammatory responses, with AMPK signaling contributing to several cellular effects. These findings support further evaluation of irisin as part of integrated prognostic assessment and investigation of irisin-related signaling in sepsis.

articles.title: Tools Measuring Health Literacy in Critically Ill Patients and Their Caregivers: A Scoping Review.
articles.abstract: Health literacy, the ability to understand and use health information, is important for critically ill patients and their caregivers in the neonatal ICU (NICU), PICU, and adult ICU to make informed decisions and navigate complex care. This review aimed to identify and summarize tools used to assess health literacy in critically ill patients or their caregivers. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and PsycINFO through July 24, 2025. Included articles reported on tools to assess health literacy in critically ill patients or their caregivers. Two reviewers independently performed screening and data extraction. Two independent reviewers extracted data in Covidence. Data items included study characteristics (country in which the study was conducted, study funding, study setting) and health literacy tool characteristics (tool user, types of questions in the tool, method of tool administration, if the tool was created by the study team, and if a full version was available in the publication). We included 92 articles describing 84 health literacy tools. Tools measured: 1) topic-specific clinical knowledge (e.g., organ donation, cardiopulmonary resuscitation; n = 24/84, 29%; NICU: n = 9; PICU: n = 1; ICU: n = 14); 2) ICU prognosis, diagnosis, and treatment (n = 23/84, 27%; NICU: 6; PICU: 3; ICU: n = 15); 3) neonatal and parenting (n = 13/84, 15%; all NICU); 4) general health literacy abilities (n = 11/84, 13%; NICU: n = 6; PICU: n = 2; ICU: n = 7); 5) information needs (n = 4/84, 5%; NICU: n = 1; PICU: n = 0; ICU: n = 3); 6) readiness for discharge (n = 3/84, 4%; all NICU); 7) decision-making (n = 3/84, 4%; all NICU); 8) health-related behaviors (n = 2/84, 2%; NICU: n = 1; ICU: n = 1); and 9) research participation (n = 1/84, 1%; NICU). Although several health literacy tools exist, they often focus on individual knowledge of specific aspects of ICU care, with less attention to how understanding is produced within the clinical context through interactions among patients, caregivers, and healthcare providers. This may limit their ability to reflect how health literacy functions in critical illness. Assessment of health literacy requires pairing the appropriate tools with interaction-focused approaches to guide communication and support informed decision-making in ICU settings.

articles.title: Pediatric Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Ventilation Rates and Outcomes.
authors: ICU-RESUS and Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Collaborative Pediatric Critical Care Research Network (CPCCRN) Investigator Groups
articles.abstract: Evaluate the association between cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) ventilation rates and survival to hospital discharge, and identify novel ventilation targets. Multicenter prospective ancillary observational cohort study of the ICU-RESUS trial (NCT02837497). A total of 18 ICUs from 10 U.S. clinical sites from October 2016 to March 2021. Hospitalized children (≤ 18 yr) with endotracheal or tracheostomy tubes and evaluable intra-arrest end-tidal carbon dioxide data to calculate ventilation rate. None. Among 234 included events, 86 events (36.8%) had guideline-recommended (20-30 beats per min [bpm]) average ventilation rates during CPR. The association between guideline-recommended CPR ventilation rate and survival to hospital discharge was evaluated with Poisson regression using generalized estimating equations, controlling for a priori covariables (initial pulse status, immediate cause of arrest). We found no association between guideline-recommended ventilation rates and survival to hospital discharge (adjusted relative risk [aRR], 0.95; 95% CI, 0.75-1.21; p = 0.68). In exploratory analyses, novel age-stratified ventilation rates were identified using natural cubic splines and subsequently evaluated in multivariable models. We identified potential thresholds (< 8 yr, ≥ 26 bpm; ≥ 8 yr, < 26 bpm). For children younger than 8 years, average CPR ventilation rate greater than or equal to 26 bpm was associated with improved survival to hospital discharge compared with less than 26 bpm (aRR, 1.32; 95% CI, 1.00-1.73; p = 0.048). CPR ventilation rates in the currently recommended range (20-30 bpm) were not associated with survival in children with in-hospital cardiac arrest. In exploratory analyses in children younger than 8 years, higher ventilation rates (≥ 26 bpm) were associated with improved survival and warrant confirmation in future studies.

Association of Oliguria With Acute Kidney Injury, Chronic Kidney Disease, and Mortality: Determining the Optimal Threshold in Critically Ill Patients.
articles.abstract: Oliguria is a key prognostic indicator of acute kidney injury (AKI), yet the consensus definition (< 0.5 mL/kg/hr) is increasingly questioned. We aimed to determine thresholds of lowest mean diuresis (LMD) associated with AKI, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and mortality. Retrospective observational study. Uppsala University Hospital ICU, Sweden. A total of 4999 adults (≥ 18 yr) without preexisting CKD admitted to the ICU between 2017 and 2024. None. LMD was calculated over 3, 6, 12, and 24 hours (LMD3h-LMD24h). Generalized additive models were used, adjusting for Simplified Acute Physiology Score 3 estimated mortality ratio and gender. Outcomes were AKI within 7 days of LMD (Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes creatinine criteria), incident CKD after ICU discharge, and 90-day mortality. All LMD time frames were significantly associated with AKI, CKD, and death (p < 0.0001). Thresholds for AKI were 0.43, 0.41, 0.42, and 0.53 mL/kg/hr; for CKD, 0.21, 0.21, 0.31, and 0.43 mL/kg/hr; and for mortality 0.16, 0.18, 0.24, and 0.39 across LMD3h-LMD24h. The risk of mortality or persistent kidney injury, reflected by incident CKD, increases at a lower urine output threshold than the current AKI definition. These findings support the idea of filtration deficit, urine output, and tissue injury as different dimensions of AKI and should influence future AKI definitions.

articles.title: Long-Lasting Mental Disorders in Caregivers of ICU Sepsis Survivors and Their Association With Patients' Post-Intensive Care Syndrome: A Prospective Multicenter Cohort Study.
authors: Investigating Long-term Outcomes of ICU patients with Sepsis or Septic shock (ILOSS) Study Group
articles.abstract: To investigate the prevalence of long-term mental disorders in caregivers of ICU sepsis survivors and examine associations with post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) in patients. Prospective observational study. Twenty-one mixed ICUs. Caregivers (the next of kin) of the patients diagnosed with sepsis between November 2020 and April 2022. None. Caregivers and patients were assessed at 3, 6, and 12 months after hospital discharge by telephone and mail. The primary outcome was caregiver mental disorders (mental post-intensive care syndrome-family [PICS-F]). Mixed-effects logistic regression analyses were performed to evaluate the association between caregiver PICS-F and patient PICS. Ninety-four caregiver-patient dyads were analyzed. Caregivers were a median of 67 years old (55-79 yr old), 31 (33.0%) were male, and 41 (43.6%) were spouses. Patients were a median of 74 years old (69-82 yr old), and 54 (57.4%) were male. The prevalence of mental PICS-F did not decrease from 3 to 12 months (43% vs. 42%, respectively), whereas the presence of PICS symptoms in patients decreased from 82% to 62%. In mixed-effects logistic regression, the presence of PICS symptoms in patients was significantly associated with PICS-F (adjusted odds ratio, 3.00; 95% CI, 1.54-5.88; p < 0.01). Among the individual patient PICS domains, only mental PICS was significantly associated with PICS-F (3.71; 2.03-6.77; p < 0.01), whereas physical and cognitive impairments in patients were not. The prevalence of mental PICS-F in caregivers of ICU sepsis survivors was frequent and long-lasting over the first year after hospital discharge. Since it was most strongly associated with patients' mental disorders rather than physical or cognitive impairments, the mental PICS domain in patients may be an important indicator of PICS-F and should be considered in future studies.

articles.title: Costs and health-related quality of life of non-operative and surgical treatment modalities for displaced distal radius fractures: a comprehensive overview based on the CAST study.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: The aim of this study was to provide a comprehensive overview of costs and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) associated with three treatment modalities for common displaced distal radius fractures (DRFs): (1) non-operative treatment, (2) direct plate fixation and (3) delayed plate fixation in case of fracture redisplacement during follow-up. A cost and HRQoL analysis was performed based on data collected during the CAST study, a multicenter cluster-randomized controlled trial including adult patients with a displaced DRF, randomized between immobilization with a plaster splint or circumferential cast. Included patients were prospectively followed for one year. Operatively treated patients also continued questionnaire follow-up. From a societal perspective, healthcare costs, patient and family costs, and indirect (i.e. productivity) costs were collected. Patients completed questionnaires on HRQoL (EQ-5D-5 L), healthcare consumption and work productivity. In total, 693 patients were included in this study (non-operative: 402, direct plate fixation: 165, delayed plate fixation: 126). The estimated mean total costs per patient were €2,212 for non-operative treatment, €4,339 for direct plate fixation and €4,393 for delayed plate fixation HRQoL improved between 3 and 12 months but did not reach pre-injury HRQoL in all groups. This study provides a descriptive overview of societal costs of displaced DRF treatment. Non-operative treatment is least costly. The cost differences between direct and delayed plate fixation is €58 in favor of direct plate fixation. Starting with non-operative treatment and later deciding whether to proceed with operative treatment based on alignment changes during follow-up, could reasonably be considered as a treatment option. HRQoL improved in all groups.

articles.title: Opsonic Peptide MOP3 Attenuates Ischemic Acute Kidney Injury.
articles.abstract: Renal ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) induced acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and serious condition characterized by renal dysfunction, inflammation, tubular injury, and cell death. Extracellular cold-inducible RNA-binding protein (eCIRP) is a damage-associated molecular pattern that contributes to inflammation and tissue injury. MFG-E8-derived oligopeptide 3 (MOP3) is an opsonic peptide that binds eCIRP and promotes its phagocytic clearance. Here, we investigated the therapeutic effects of MOP3 in a murine model of renal I/R-induced AKI. Mice were subjected to 30 minutes of bilateral renal ischemia and treated with MOP3 or vehicle at the onset of reperfusion. Blood and kidney tissues were collected 20 h later. Renal inflammation, kidney function, tubular injury markers, histological damage, and cell death were assessed by RT-qPCR, biochemical assays, Western blotting, hematoxylin and eosin staining, and TUNEL staining. MOP3 treatment reduced circulating eCIRP by 40% and renal IL-6, IL-1β, MIP-2, and KC mRNA expression by 43%, 84%, 73%, and 69%, respectively, compared with vehicle treatment. Serum urea nitrogen, creatinine, and NGAL levels were reduced by 56%, 63%, and 44%, respectively, after MOP3 treatment. MOP3 also decreased renal KIM-1 and NGAL mRNA expression by 88% and 44% and reduced their protein levels by 29% and 45%, respectively. Furthermore, MOP3 attenuated renal tubular injury and decreased TUNEL-positive cells. These findings demonstrate that MOP3 attenuates inflammation, renal dysfunction, tubular injury, and cell death following renal I/R, suggesting that MOP3 may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for ischemic AKI.

articles.title: Fibrinolytic Activation and Its Association with Mortality After Traumatic and Thermal Injury.
articles.abstract: Characterize plasma markers of fibrinolytic activation and their associations with mortality in burn and trauma patients from hospital admission through 48 hours. Fibrinolytic activation following burn and non-burn trauma is associated with increased mortality. Whether fibrinolytic activation differs between burn and non-burn injury is unknown. Adult patients aged 18 years and older who presented to one of two regional trauma centers or one regional burn center within 4 hours of injury were included. Blood was collected at admission and at hours 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, 36, and 48. Plasmin-antiplasmin complex (PAP), D-dimer, and plasminogen concentrations in plasma were determined. Of 590 patients, 58.3% presented with blunt, 27.1% with thermal, and 14.6% with penetrating injury. Admission PAP and D-dimer were higher in trauma (blunt and penetrating groups combined) than in burn patients (p<.001). Non-survivors (injury types combined) had higher PAP and D-dimer and lower plasminogen (p<.001) at admission and over time. After adjusting for age, injury severity and % total body surface area burned, admission PAP ≥1645.6 ng/mL was associated with 7.0 times higher odds for mortality (p=.002) and D-dimer ≥6.5 µg/mL was associated with 5.0 times higher odds for mortality (p=.01). Changes in biomarkers over time were similar between trauma and burn patients. Higher fibrinolytic activation was associated with mortality in trauma and burn patients. Trauma patients had higher fibrinolytic activation markers than burn patients, while patterns of change were similar. Data suggest potential for use of similar resuscitative adjuncts to mitigate early fibrinolytic dysfunction in trauma and burns.

Dominant lung involvement and heterozygous IFIH1 variants.
articles.abstract: Heterozygous gain-of-function (GoF) variants in IFIH1 are associated with rare autoinflammatory diseases characterized by heightened interferons-stimulated gene (ISG) signatures. These include Aicardi-Goutières syndrome, presenting with slowly progressive spastic paraparesis of the lower limbs, intracerebral calcifications, and neuroinflammation, and Singleton-Merten syndrome, defined by tooth loss, bone demineralization, and vascular calcification. Do rare IFIH1 GoF variants contribute to an interstitial lung disease phenotype, thereby expanding the spectrum of IFIH1-related disorders? Among 559 children with interstitial lung disease (chILD) and exome sequencing as part of their diagnostic work-up, 12 rare heterozygous IFIH1 variants were identified. Of these, 10 were missense variants of unknown significance, which were functionally assessed in vitro using luciferase assay and ISG-expression profiling. Genome-wide RNA analysis was performed on available patient samples to explore broader transcriptional effects. Four variants with increased basal IFNβ transcription in vitro and elevated ISG expression in vivo indicating GoF behaviour were identified. Disease severity correlated with GoF potential of the respective variant. Two patients harbouring IFIH1 variants with strong GoF activity displayed multisystem involvement and died from respiratory failure at 3 and 4 months of age, respectively. Two additional patients showed milder phenotypes with chronic lung disease stabilizing by the age of 8 and 10 years, respectively. Lung biopsies showed alveolar hypoplasia and alveolar macrophage pneumonia (=desquamative interstitial pneumonia) of varying severity. We report a dominant interstitial lung disease phenotype in individuals harbouring novel IFIH1 variants, expanding IFIH1-related disease to the group of type I interferonopathies with pulmonary manifestations like STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy (SAVI) and COPA syndrome.

articles.title: Mechanical versus manual bag-valve ventilation during cardiopulmonary resuscitation in adults with cardiac arrest: A systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Optimal ventilation delivery during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) remains uncertain. Current resuscitation guidelines do not recommend mechanical ventilation (MV) over manual bag-valve ventilation (BV). We evaluated the association between MV use during CPR and clinical outcomes in adults with cardiac arrest compared with manual BV. We searched 6 bibliographic databases from inception through May 31, 2026. Included studies compared MV and BV ventilation CPR in adult cardiac arrest patients. Patients receiving MV at any moment during CPR were classified as the MV group; those receiving only BV comprised the BV group. Primary outcomes included return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to hospital admission, survival to hospital discharge, and good neurological outcome. Secondary outcomes included physiologic variables and pneumothorax. We calculated pooled risk ratios (RRs) and mean differences with 95% credible intervals (CrIs) using Bayesian random-effects meta-analyses. Eight studies involving 6,847 patients were included. For the primary outcome, MV use during CPR was associated with a higher rate of ROSC than BV use (pooled RR, 1.20; 95% CrI, 1.04 to 1.42), with a 99% posterior probability of benefit. Posterior probabilities favoring MV for survival to admission, survival to discharge, and favorable neurological outcome were 92.3%, 93.6%, and 92.2%, respectively. Pneumothorax incidence was similar between groups. In adult cardiac arrest, MV use during CPR was associated with higher ROSC compared with manual BV. Evidence for improved survival and neurological outcomes remains imprecise and inconclusive.

articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Traumatic hemothorax is a common consequence of thoracic injury, with management strategies ranging from observation to tube thoracostomy and operative intervention. This Western Trauma Association algorithm provides a practical framework for the evaluation and management of patients with traumatic hemothorax. Recommendations were developed through review of the available literature, including randomized and observational studies, supplemented by expert consensus where high-quality evidence is limited. The proposed pathway incorporates patient physiology, hemothorax size, adequacy of pleural drainage, and evidence of ongoing hemorrhage to guide management decisions. Because clinical circumstances, institutional resources, and local practice patterns vary, the algorithm is intended to support rather than replace individualized clinical judgment. It may be used as a bedside reference and as a framework for the development of institution-specific protocols. Consensus algorithm from the Western Trauma Association; Level V.

articles.title: Reductions in PTSD symptom clusters among perinatal and postnatal survivors of intimate partner violence participating in the Heartbeats program.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Intimate partner violence (IPV) remains a leading cause of injury among women, especially during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Experiencing IPV increases the risk of mental health disorders, including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). PTSD during the perinatal period is associated with poorer maternal mental health and adverse early child outcomes. Heartbeats (HB) is a hospital-based, community-linked violence intervention program designed to reduce morbidity and mortality among perinatal and postnatal survivors of IPV. HB provides crisis intervention, intensive case management, and counseling to pregnant patients up to 2 years postpartum who have experienced IPV. Given the high burden of mental health concerns in this population, a primary goal of HB is to reduce PTSD symptoms. This study was conducted at a Level 1 trauma center. Participants were identified through IPV-related injury presentations, routine hospital screening, or referrals. Seventy-four participants completed the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) at intake (baseline) and 4 months postbaseline (follow-up). Total PTSD and subscale scores were calculated for intrusion (re-experiencing), avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and alterations in arousal and reactivity (hyperarousal). Paired-samples t tests assessed changes from baseline to follow-up. Significant reductions were observed in total PTSD symptoms (M=9.16, SD=23.64, p=0.003) and across all subscales: intrusion (re-experiencing; M=2.76, SD=6.19, p<0.001), avoidance (M=1.18, SD=2.90, p<0.001), negative alterations in cognition and mood (M=3.82, SD=8.83, p<0.001), and alterations in arousal and reactivity (hyperarousal; M=2.33, SD=7.25, p=0.008). HB program participation was associated with significant reductions in overall PTSD severity and each DSM-5 symptom cluster. These findings support the potential of integrated hospital-based, community-linked programs to improve trauma recovery outcomes among perinatal survivors of IPV. Prognostic/Epidemiologic; Level III.

Effectiveness of Continuous Automatic Endotracheal Cuff Pressure Monitoring in Preventing Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is a major healthcare-associated infection in critically ill children, primarily driven by microaspiration around the endotracheal tube cuff. Does continuous automatic cuff pressure monitoring (CACPM) reduce the incidence of VAP compared to intermittent manual cuff pressure monitoring (IMCPM) in critically ill pediatric patients requiring mechanical ventilation? In this open-label, randomized controlled superiority trial, pediatric patients requiring mechanical ventilation for ≥48 hours were randomly assigned (1:1) to either CACPM or IMCPM. The target cuff pressure was strictly maintained at 20-25 cmH2O. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients developing VAP within 28 days following intubation, evaluated in the intention to treat population. Secondary outcomes included time to VAP diagnosis and target pressure compliance. Statistical approaches included Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and multivariable Cox proportional hazard regression. Among 241 randomized patients, ITT analysis showed lower VAP with CACPM than IMCPM (13.3% vs 24.0%; risk difference, -10.6 percentage points; 95% CI, -20.3 to -0.8; P=0.034), with similar PP findings (15.0% vs 26.6%; P=0.044). ITT incidence density was 15.7 vs 27.1 per 1,000 ventilator-days (IRR, 1.73; 95% CI, 0.94-3.18; P=0.080). Unadjusted time-to-VAP was nonsignificant (HR, 1.80; 95% CI, 0.976-3.321; P=0.060), whereas adjusted Cox analysis narrowly indicated a higher VAP hazard with IMCPM (HR, 1.90; 95% CI, 1.024-3.510; P=0.042). Target-pressure compliance was higher with CACPM (P<0.001). CACPM significantly reduces the proportion of critically ill pediatric patients developing VAP compared with IMCPM. This preventive effect appears directly linked to improved target pressure compliance, suggesting that automated regulation could be a valuable addition to pediatric VAP prevention strategies. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05918172.

articles.title: The Cost-Effectiveness and Health Equity of Prehospital Treatment Strategies for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Patients: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a major public health challenge, associated with substantial mortality and significant costs for health care system. This systematic review aimed to (i) synthesize economic evaluations of prehospital treatment strategies for OHCA from ambulance attendance through to hospital discharge; (ii) assess the methodological quality and reporting of the included studies; and (iii) evaluate the reporting of health equity-relevant data. We searched Medline, Embase, Scopus, EconLit, and CINAHL databases for records from database inception to 12 June 2026. The QHES and CHEERS checklists were used to assess the quality and reporting standards of included studies, and the review was reported according to the PRISMA checklist. The completeness of reporting health equity outcomes was reviewed using the PROGRESS (Place of residence, Race, Occupation, Gender, Religion, Education, Socioeconomic status and Social capital) - Plus framework. Ten economic evaluations met eligibility criteria. Most studies were cost-utility analyses (n = 8, 80%) and used Markov models (n = 6, 60%). Most evaluations were 'very good quality' (≥80%) (n = 6, 60%). Early defibrillation and advanced life support (ALS) delivered by trained emergency medical technicians were cost-effective compared with no intervention, emergency physician-led ALS, standard emergency medical services or paramedic care (ICER range from £11,407 to USD $56,700 per QALY gained). Prehospital extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) was more cost-effective than in-hospital ECPR strategies (ICER range from AUD $27,323 to $44,000 per QALY gained). Termination-of-resuscitation (TOR) strategies were cost-effective compared with no TOR or other TOR strategies, including basic life support and ALS TOR, with estimates of $110,554 saved per QALY lost and USD $23,851 per QALY gained. Survival rate and neurological outcomes influenced cost-effectiveness results. Equity reporting was limited: almost all included studies addressed less than 40% of the PROGRESS-Plus equity criteria. Most strategies that increased prehospital treatment intensity, avoided futile transport, or enabled earlier advanced care were cost-effective; however, the certainty of evidence, particularly for sub-groups, was limited by heterogeneous comparators and sparse equity reporting.

Designing a hybrid surgical ICU to avoid intrahospital transport in selected critically Ill patients: the CUHK-SZ institutional concept.
articles.journal: World journal of emergency surgery : WJES
articles.abstract: Intrahospital transport for surgery exposes critically ill patients to equipment failure, displacement of tubes and lines, interrupted monitoring, and physiologic instability. Although transport protocols can reduce these hazards, they do not address the underlying physical decoupling of surgical infrastructure from the critical care environment. This institutional perspective describes the rationale and design of a hybrid surgical ICU planned for the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen (CUHK-SZ) Medical Center: a dedicated clinical space designed to function as both a critical care unit and a procedural suite, bringing surgery to the patient rather than transporting the patient to the operating room (OR). The model is presented as an illustrative, hypothesis-generating concept rather than a validated clinical pathway. The design concept, which is a patient-centered approach, should guide healthcare delivery in modern medicine by placing the patient at the forefront of all decisions and mobilizing all available resources to serve them. This approach addresses all three domains: personnel, environment, and equipment. Overlapping anesthesiology and critical care competencies support integrated staffing. Connectable ICU rooms, adequate space and electrical capacity, anterooms, and switchable HEPA-filtered positive-pressure ventilation meet environmental requirements. Total intravenous anesthesia, portable surgical platforms, and minimally invasive or robotic techniques reduce dependence on fixed OR infrastructure. At CUHK-SZ, the concept is planned as a prototype in the trauma building using two adjacent ICU rooms with an openable partition and switchable ventilation. Candidate patient groups, procedural levels, and implementation requirements are presented as provisional, expert-derived proposals, and engineering testing and simulated drills are planned before any clinical use. The hybrid surgical ICU is a technically plausible option for carefully selected patients at high risk from transport, but its clinical effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness remain unproven. The CUHK-SZ concept is intended to generate hypotheses for prospective evaluation, and its transferability to existing hospitals is likely to depend on incremental adaptation rather than direct replication.

articles.title: Switching from mepolizumab to benralizumab in eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA).
authors: European EGPA study group (EESG) and the French Vasculitis Study Group (FVSG)
articles.abstract: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is an ANCA-associated vasculitis characterized by eosinophilic asthma and ENT involvement. Both mepolizumab and benralizumab have demonstrated efficacy in EGPA and are now considered front-line options. In patients who do not respond to mepolizumab, benralizumab may be a valuable alternative owing to its enhanced depletion of eosinophils. We assessed the efficacy for and safety of switching from mepolizumab to benralizumab in EGPA. Is benralizumab effective and safe in EGPA patients after mepolizumab failure, given its enhanced depletion of eosinophil? We conducted a retrospective European multicenter study including 68 adult EGPA patients who received benralizumab after mepolizumab failure. Complete (CR) and partial (PR) response were defined as BVAS=0, with prednisone ≤4 mg/day and > 4 mg/day, respectively. Median benralizumab follow-up period was 28 [20-39] months. CR and PR were achieved in 32% and 25% of patients, and maintained at last follow-up in 19% and 16%. Median time to CR was 6 [4-12] months. Forced expiratory volume in one second improved from 73% to 79%, and 38% of patients discontinued glucocorticoids. Vasculitis flares occurred in six patients. Primary mepolizumab failure was associated with lower CR rates (OR 0.19, 95% CI 0.06-0.60). Benralizumab was discontinued in 18% due to persistent respiratory symptoms. Adverse events occurred in five patients, including two severe SARS-CoV-2 infections. In EGPA patients with persistent respiratory manifestations after mepolizumab failure, switching to benralizumab could represent a valuable option, improving lung function and reducing glucocorticoid use. Further prospective studies are needed to optimize sequencing and patient selection.

articles.title: Early Post-ROSC Laboratory Phenotypes and Clinical Outcomes after Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A 10-Year National Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Prior phenotyping in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) relied predominantly on prehospital indicators, which neither describe nor grade the underlying ischemia-reperfusion injury. We aimed to derive laboratory-based phenotypes and describe their clinical characteristics and outcome associations. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adult resuscitated OHCA patients of presumed cardiac etiology between 01/02/2011 and 01/01/2022, linking Singapore's national OHCA and cardiovascular databases. Unsupervised latent class analysis (LCA) was applied to 14 laboratory variables within six hours post-return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Stability was confirmed through split-sample validation. Logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards model, adjusted for age, sex and initial cardiac rhythm, assessed poor neurological recovery at hospital discharge, 30-day and 3-year mortality. Among 1514 eligible patients (median age 65.0 years, 73.6% males), LCA identified three distinct phenotypes: multi-organ dysfunction (MOD, N=286), homeostatic (HOM, N=967), and immune-dysregulated (IMD, N=261), independently reproduced in derivation (entropy=0.817) and replication (entropy=0.892) subsamples. The most discriminative variables were creatinine, eosinophil and lymphocyte. Compared to MOD, both HOM (aOR: 0.50, 95% CI 0.30-0.78, p=0.004) and IMD (aOR: 0.46, 95% CI 0.26-0.78, p=0.005) phenotypes had significantly lower odds of poor neurological recovery. This pattern was consistent for 30-day mortality (HOM aHR: 0.71, 95% CI 0.61-0.83; IMD aHR: 0.78, 95% CI 0.64-0.94) and 3-year mortality (HOM aHR: 0.70, 95% CI 0.60-0.82; IMD aHR: 0.74, 95% CI 0.62-0.90), all p≤0.01. Early post-ROSC laboratory data identified three prognostically distinct phenotypes among resuscitated OHCA patients. These exploratory findings support external validation and investigation of phenotype-guided therapies.

articles.title: The Epidemiology of Paediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in Australia and New Zealand: A Report from The Australasian Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium Epistry (Aus-ROC).
articles.abstract: This first epidemiological study of paediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (pOHCA) across Australia and New Zealand explores the incidence, patient and event characteristics, both overall and by developmental age groups, and examines factors associated with outcomes. All pOHCAs (aged <18 years) attended by emergency medical services (EMS) in Australia and New Zealand from 2017 to 2023 were included. Crude incidence rates (per 100,000 person-years) were calculated for EMS-attended and EMS-treated cases. Logistic regression models were used to identify associations between patient and arrest characteristics and survival (event and 30-day/hospital discharge). EMS attended 4,779 cases and treated 3,139 (65.7%). Incidence rates for EMS-attended and EMS-treated cases were 10.1 and 6.6, respectively; with a bimodal age distribution peaking in infants (65.4) and adolescents (11.4). Most EMS-attended cases were unwitnessed (66.9%), of medical origin (60.1%), had initial non-shockable rhythms (91.1%), occurred in private residences (74.3%), and received bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (62.7%). Few (1.6%) received bystander defibrillation. Arrest characteristics varied widely between age groups. Survival to 30-days/hospital discharge in EMS-treated cases was 10.0% (highest in late childhood [15.4%] and lowest in infants [7.9%]). Multivariable analysis identified that increasing age was positively associated with event survival, whilst bystander-witnessed arrest, initial shockable rhythm, arrest aetiology, and EMS response time were significant predictors of short and long-term survival. The incidence, patient characteristics, and survival outcomes of pOHCA in our region differ significantly by age groups. Age- and context-specific prevention and resuscitation strategies are essential for reducing the burden and improving survival outcomes.

articles.title: Opioid-Associated vs Undifferentiated Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Examining differences in outcomes and the relationship with Utstein variables.
articles.abstract: The pathophysiology of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) due to opioid toxicity is different from other OHCAs. Our aims were to determine: (1) whether opioid-toxicity is associated with OHCA outcomes; and, (2) whether the relationship between Utstein variables and outcomes differ between those with opioid-associated (OA) and other OHCA. We analysed adult emergency medical services (EMS)-treated OHCAs from the British Columbia Cardiac Arrest Registry. Using post-mortem toxicological investigations, death certificates, and hospital-based diagnoses, we classified as OA-OHCA or "undifferentiated OHCA". We fit a multivariable logistic regression model to assess the association between OA-OHCA (versus undifferentiated OHCA) and favourable neurological outcome at hospital discharge. We then added pre-specified interaction terms to individual models for: sex, initial cardiac rhythm, bystander CPR, witnessed arrest, and location type. Of 10,786 OHCAs: 1349 (13%) were OA-OHCA, of whom 331 (25%) were female, and the median age was 40 years (IQR 31-50); 9437 (87%) were undifferentiated, of whom 2910 (31%) were female, and the median age was 70 years (IQR 58-81). We did not detect an association between OA-OHCA (OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.77, 1.35) and survival with favourable neurological outcomes. Models adding interaction terms demonstrated statistically significant interactions for: sex (p=0.032), initial cardiac rhythm (p=0.024), and bystander-witnessed status (p=<0.001). Overall, we did not detect an association between opioid toxicity and outcomes. In models with interaction terms, the relationship between Utstein and outcomes differed between opioid-associated and other OHCAs, highlighting the impact opioid-associated cases may have in observational OHCA analyses.

articles.title: Survival benefit of prehospital TXA in fibrinolytic shutdown: Insights from two prospective trauma trials.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Fibrinolytic phenotypes have been implicated in postinjury pathophysiology and outcomes. While prehospital tranexamic acid (TXA) administration has demonstrated survival benefits, the interaction between TXA administration and distinct fibrinolytic profiles remains poorly defined. We analyzed data from a harmonized dataset combining 2 prospective trials evaluating prehospital TXA use in trauma (Prehospital Tranexamic Acid Use for Traumatic Brain Injury and the Study of Tranexamic Acid During Air and Ground Medical Prehospital Transport Trial). Patients were stratified by initial thromboelastographic (TEG) LY30 into fibrinolytic shutdown (<0.9%), hyperfibrinolysis (>3%), and physiological fibrinolysis (0.9-3%). The primary outcome was 30-day mortality. Secondary outcomes included 24-hour mortality and adverse events. Multivariable regression adjusted for TXA administration, fibrinolysis phenotypes, age, mechanism of injury, injury severity score, and shock index on presentation to the hospital. Among 1,249 patients, 30-day mortality was 14.5% in the fibrinolytic shutdown group, 6.7% in the hyperfibrinolysis group, and 6.5% in the physiological fibrinolysis group. After multivariable regression, hyperfibrinolysis was associated with increased risk of death (HR 2.87; 95% CI: 1.10-7.53; p 0.03). Patients with fibrinolytic shutdown who were randomized to TXA had decreased risk of death (HR 0.32; 95% CI: 0.11-0.91; p=0.03). This multitrial analysis revealed greater statistically significant differences between fibrinolytic phenotypes than analysis of each trial alone. Fibrinolytic phenotypes were independently associated with mortality. Fibrinolytic shutdown in patients randomized to receive TXA was associated with lower risk of death. These findings support the relevance of fibrinolysis profiling during early trauma care and underscore the need for larger studies to further elucidate the prognostic and therapeutic implications in trauma. II (Subanalysis of Randomized Controlled Trials).

articles.title: Decompressive craniectomy: The potential association with long-term functional outcomes in children with traumatic brain injury.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is the leading cause of death and disability in pediatric patients. However, TBI management widely varies due to a lack of high-quality evidence in pediatric population. We aimed to determine the association of decompressive craniectomy (DC) on long-term functional independence in pediatric TBI. We hypothesize that the use of DC would not be associated with improved functional independence after discharge. This is a retrospective cohort study using the Federal Interagency Traumatic Brain Injury Research (FITBIR) Informatics System, a national database of TBI studies. The Approaches and Decisions in Acute Pediatric TBI (ADAPT) Trial was selected for its international patient population from 2014 to 2017. Patients (age ≤18 y) with TBI, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) ≤8, and insertion of an intracranial pressure monitor were categorized into the DC and no-DC groups. The primary outcome was Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended Pediatric Version (GOS-E Peds) at a follow-up visit ≥6 months postdischarge. A secondary analysis included all patients admitted for the management of TBI to examine the association between DC and in-hospital mortality. We included 686 TBI patients followed up ≥6 months postdischarge or recorded mortality. Of those, 213 (31.0%) patients received DC. The median GCS on presentation was 5. The median GOS-E at follow-up was 5. In a multivariate regression model, the use of DC was not associated with good functional recovery defined as GOS-E Peds <5 (odds ratio [OR]: 0.64, 95% CI: 0.39-1.05, p=0.077). In a secondary analysis, DC was not associated with in-hospital mortality (OR: 1.02, 95% CI: 0.60-1.74, p=0.95). The results of this study suggest that DC is not significantly associated with favorable functional outcomes >6 months postdischarge or decreased in-hospital mortality. Future research is warranted to further delineate the indication for DC in the pediatric TBI population. Prognostic/epidemiological study; Level IV.

articles.title: Does Surgeon Experience Affect Outcomes in Robotic Cholecystectomy for Emergency Biliary Disease? A Statewide Analysis.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: The use of robotic surgery (RS) as an operative technique in emergency general surgery (EGS) is rapidly growing, with a >3-fold increase in RS-EGS operations since 2011. Prior work has utilized payer claims to evaluate outcomes of RS-cholecystectomy in the EGS setting. However, these studies fail to evaluate how outcomes are affected by surgeon experience or whether there is a learning curve for RS in the EGS setting. We hypothesized that surgeons on the learning curve may have higher rates of complications. EGS collaborative data from 12 hospitals were used to compare the postoperative outcomes of patients undergoing RS-cholecystectomy to those undergoing laparoscopic (LS) cholecystectomy. Unadjusted and adjusted outcomes were compared between the control (LS) and the exposure (RS) groups, using entropy balancing and multivariable analysis. Learning curves were plotted for postoperative outcomes, operative time, and hospital length of stay, using linear spline curve modeling (single knot at case 70) to represent how outcomes change with increasing surgeon experience. We evaluated 8,221 minimally invasive total cholecystectomy cases, of which 2,141 were performed with RS. RS-cholecystectomy was associated with a lower rate of technical complications, independent of surgeon experience (adjusted odds ratio: 0.38, 95% CI: 0.21-0.69, p=0.002). Operative time was longer, and nontechnical complications were higher for RS-cholecystectomy (+13.1min, 95% CI: 7.3-18.8, p<0.001 and adjusted odds ratio: 1.18, 95% CI: 1.01-1.39, P=0.043, respectively). Adjusted operative time decreased by 14.1 minutes over the first 70 cases (95% CI: -21.8 to -6.4, p<0.001). RS-cholecystectomy is not associated with more technical complications, and surgeons with less RS experience did not have a higher likelihood of technical complications for cholecystectomy when compared with LS in an EGS setting. Operative times for RS-cholecystectomy are longer than LS and significantly decrease with increasing surgeon experience. Therapeutic/Care Management; Level III. Prognostic/epidemiological.

articles.title: A Simple Platelet-Centered Coagulation-Inflammation Combined Score for Predicting In-Hospital Mortality in Sepsis.
articles.abstract: Accurate mortality prediction in sepsis requires assessing coagulation and inflammatory disturbances, yet existing scores are complex or incompletely capture these interconnected processes. We developed and internally validated a simple score combining inflammatory and platelet-related indicators with clinical parameters to predict in-hospital mortality in sepsis. This retrospective study included 6175 adults with sepsis from the MIMIC-IV database. Patients were randomly divided into training (n=4322) and validation (n=1853) cohorts. Candidate predictors were screened by least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression, and final variables entered multivariable logistic regression to construct the Coagulation-Inflammation Combined Score (CICS). Performance was assessed by discrimination, calibration, internal bootstrap validation, and decision curve analysis. Of 6175 patients, 807 (13.1%) died during hospitalization. The final CICS incorporated five routinely available variables: lactate, Glasgow Coma Scale score, age, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, and platelet count. Discrimination was good, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.768 (95% CI, 0.747-0.788) in training and 0.806 (95% CI, 0.776-0.835) in validation cohorts, comparable to SOFA (DeLong P=0.526 and P=0.180). Calibration was acceptable (Brier scores 0.102 and 0.091). Bootstrap validation indicated minimal optimism, and decision curve analysis showed exploratory findings across clinically relevant thresholds. The CICS is a parsimonious prognostic score using five routinely available variables from the first 24 hours after ICU admission. It showed discrimination comparable to SOFA, acceptable calibration, and favorable decision-curve performance. CICS should be interpreted as a separate prognostic score for early ICU stratification once first-24-hour data are available, rather than for emergency department triage or ICU admission decisions.

Outcomes Following Impedance Threshold Device Use During Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
articles.abstract: Existing work is equivocal regarding the benefit of impedance threshold device (ITD) use among patients experiencing out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). We examined the association of ITD use with prehospital outcomes and longer-term dispositions in a nationally representative sample of OHCA patients. We included adult, non-traumatic, OHCA scene runs from the 2024 ESO Data Collaborative. We compared patients treated with (a) ITD only; (b) ITD and active compression-decompression device (ITD+ACD); and (c) neither device (no ITD). Prehospital outcomes included return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and survival to hospital arrival (SHA); disposition outcomes included survival to hospital discharge and favorable neurologic outcome (i.e., discharge to home). We used multivariate logistic regression to examine the association of treatment group with outcomes, adjusting for demographics and several potential confounders. We included 97,439 patient records (85.3% no ITD; 13.1% ITD only; 1.6% ITD+ACD). Disposition outcomes were available for 13,026 patients (23.3%). ROSC was higher for patients treated with ITD only (26.7%) than those treated with no ITD (23.8%; aOR=1.09 [1.04, 1.14]); a similar pattern emerged for SHA. Conversely, survival to discharge was lower for patients treated with ITD only (23.9%) than those treated with no ITD (32.0%; aOR=0.68, [.61, .76]); a similar pattern emerged for favorable neurologic outcome. The ITD+ACD group showed more extreme versions of the trends observed for ITD only. ITD use was associated with improved prehospital outcomes but worsened dispositional outcomes among patients experiencing OHCA, suggesting this device may prove beneficial early in resuscitation of OHCA patients.

articles.title: Non-invasive respiratory supports in ARDS: Physiology-guided use, pitfalls, and pathways to success.
Training for humanization in intensive care: a competency-based educational continuum for patient- and family-centred practice.
Distinctive patterns in child homicide: A retrospective study in Maryland.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Homicide is a leading cause of childhood death, yet few studies distinguish child homicide from adolescent and adult patterns, challenging the development of prevention strategies. We sought to define how child homicide epidemiology differs from that of older age groups in Maryland. In this cross-sectional study, we analyzed all homicide decedents in Maryland (2005-2017) using Office of the Chief Medical Examiner data. Age groups were defined per American Academy of Pediatrics: child/early adolescent (0-14), adolescent (15-22), young adult (23-30), and adult (31+). Descriptive statistics were calculated, and multinomial logistic regression (children as reference) assessed associations with sex, race, mechanism, site, and geography. Two interactions (race×sex and mechanism×site) were retained. Among 6,508 homicide decedents, 217 were children, 1,242 adolescents, 2,226 young adults, and 2,823 adults. Children were more often female (44% vs. 9%-19%) and less likely to die in Baltimore (25% vs. 40%-46%) than all older groups, and more likely to die at home (21% vs. 5%-7%) than adolescents and young adults. Firearm deaths were less common in children (28% vs. 65%-84%) while blunt trauma was more common (36% vs. 2%-9%). In regression, older groups were less likely than children to be female (OR, 0.6-0.8), die at home (OR, 0.1-0.5, p<0.05) if killed by firearms, or die outside Baltimore (OR, 0.5-0.6, p<0.01). Significant race × sex interactions were observed for Black female decedents across older age groups (interaction ORs, 0.2-0.4; all p<0.05). Significant mechanism × site interactions were also observed, including Blunt × Home (interaction OR, 32.7; p<0.001) and Strangulation × Home (interaction OR, 48.4; p=0.001) among adults. Child homicide differs markedly from older groups, with victims more often female, killed by non-firearm mechanisms, at home, and outside Baltimore. By adolescence, decedents reflect a more "adult" profile in sex, mechanism, site, and geography. Homicide prevention strategies for children may need to diverge from those targeting community gun violence in older groups. (J Trauma Acute Care Surg. 2026;00: 000-000. articles.title: Spectral Characteristics and Parameters of Pulse Oximetry Waveforms for Assessing Resuscitation Status.
articles.abstract: Real-time assessment of physiological resuscitation status is critical for guiding personalised cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and avoiding unnecessary harm from prolonged chest compressions. Non-invasive, objectively trackable tools for this purpose remain limited. This multicentre retrospective study (2013-2018) included 451 adult patients with cardiac arrest (497 CPR episodes) from 14 Chinese tertiary hospitals, comprising 158 Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (OHCA) episodes with prehospital SpO2/ECG monitoring continued upon ED arrival and full pulse oximetry plethysmography (POP)/ECG/end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2) monitoring established in the ED, and 339 In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (IHCA) episodes occurring in the ED. We analysed POP waveforms across four statuses: compression-only (CC), chest compression with return of spontaneous circulation (CC+ROSC, spontaneous circulation during ongoing compressions), non-compression without ROSC, and spontaneous circulation-only (SC). Time-domain (area under the POP curve [POPAUC]) and frequency-domain spectral features were evaluated against clinically documented ROSC. A frequency-domain "hybrid" pattern during the CC+ROSC identified ROSC with 100% specificity (PPV 1.000). In CC status,POPAUC was higher in stable-ROSC than unstable-ROSC (3232.2±1008.2 vs. 2769.6±1013.0 PVPG, P=0.007). The POPAUC was lower in CC+ROSC status than in SC status for stable-ROSC (2768.2±997.8 vs. 3335.8±842.4 PVPG, P=0.001), but the reverse was observed for unstable-ROSC (2697.5±941.0 vs. 1338.1±952.6 PVPG, P<0.001). POP waveforms disappearance with concurrent ECG presence identified pulseless electrical activity with 100% specificity. Pulse oximetry plethysmography waveform analysis-using signals already available on standard monitors-may provide a non-invasive, real-time approach that may help identify ROSC during ongoing compressions and distinguish between stable and unstable circulation.

articles.title: Race and Ethnicity Are Associated With Physical Impairment Among ICU Survivors.
articles.abstract: To evaluate whether race and ethnicity are associated with increased odds of physical impairment among post-ICU survivors and to assess how impairment influences healthcare utilization after hospital discharge. This was a retrospective cohort study. The study was conducted at an academic medical center. We included 4370 adult ICU survivors who experienced shock, respiratory failure, or received extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. None. The primary exposure was self-reported race and ethnicity. The primary outcome was impairment at hospital discharge, defined using the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision codes and/or a Johns Hopkins Highest Level of Mobility score of less than or equal to 5. Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess associations with impairment, and Fine-Gray models evaluated post-discharge healthcare utilization. Impairment was identified in 31% of ICU survivors. Non-Hispanic Black race was associated with increased odds of any impairment (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.34; 95% CI, 1.04-1.72), and Hispanic ethnicity was associated with increased odds of new impairment (aOR, 1.42; 95% CI, 1.05-1.91), compared with non-Hispanic White-identifying survivors. Among those with impairment, both non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic individuals had increased risk of healthcare utilization within 1 year. Non-Hispanic Black race and Hispanic ethnicity are associated with increased odds of post-ICU physical impairment and subsequent healthcare utilization. These findings highlight the need to understand root causes better and explore targeted interventions to reduce disparities among ICU survivors.

articles.title: Apixaban vs rivaroxaban for venous thromboembolism: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Direct oral anticoagulants are first-line therapy for venous thromboembolism (VTE), yet comparative evidence between apixaban and rivaroxaban remains limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of apixaban versus rivaroxaban in patients with VTE. A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library was conducted from inception through March 2026. Studies directly comparing apixaban and rivaroxaban in adult VTE patients were included. Outcomes, including recurrent VTE, major bleeding, all-cause mortality, and net clinical harm, were pooled using a random-effects model. Thirteen studies comprising more than 220,000 patients were included. Apixaban was associated with a significantly lower risk of recurrent VTE compared to rivaroxaban (RR 0.85; 95% CI 0.74-0.98), with moderate heterogeneity. Apixaban was also associated with a significant 28% reduction in major bleeding risk (RR 0.72; 95% CI 0.65-0.81), with low heterogeneity, indicating consistent findings across studies. When efficacy and safety outcomes were combined, apixaban demonstrated a significantly lower risk of net clinical harm (RR 0.76; 95% CI 0.68-0.86). In contrast, no statistically significant difference was observed in all-cause mortality (RR 0.95; 95% CI 0.80-1.12), with substantial heterogeneity across studies. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these findings, with no single study significantly altering the overall estimates. Overall, apixaban demonstrated a more favorable efficacy and safety profile compared with rivaroxaban in VTE management, with reduced recurrence and bleeding risk, while mortality remained comparable. These findings suggest that apixaban may be associated with a more favorable efficacy and safety profile than rivaroxaban; however, the results should be interpreted cautiously given the predominance of observational evidence.

articles.title: Diagnostic accuracy of shock index, revised trauma score, and injury severity score for mortality prediction in trauma: A hierarchical meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Shock Index (SI) and Revised Trauma Score (RTS) are physiological tools available at the point of trauma triage. Injury Severity Score (ISS) is an anatomical score that requires completed injury characterization and is typically available only after initial resuscitation. Their comparative value for predicting mortality and whether ISS meaningfully adds to the acute tools remains unclear. The aim of this systematic review and hierarchical meta-analysis is to pool the diagnostic accuracy of SI and RTS as acute mortality-prediction tools in adult trauma patients; to benchmark these against ISS; and to formally test, in studies reporting both, whether RTS and ISS differ in diagnostic accuracy. Electronic databases were searched from inception to May 2026. In-hospital mortality was prespecified as the primary endpoint. Pooled sensitivity, specificity and hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) analyses were performed with a bivariate random-effects model for each tool separately. For studies reporting both RTS and ISS in the same cohort, a paired comparison was performed using a bivariate model with test type as a covariate and a pooled within-study difference analysis. Twelve studies (234,129 patients) were included. Pooled sensitivity/specificity were 0.679/0.763 for SI (5 studies, AUC 0.747), 0.788/0.801 for RTS (6 studies, AUC 0.852), and 0.788/0.796 for ISS (9 studies, AUC 0.855). In the six studies reporting both RTS and ISS, a paired bivariate comparison found no significant difference in diagnostic accuracy (likelihood-ratio test, p = 0.91; within-study sensitivity OR 1.59, 95% CI 0.82-3.07; specificity OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.55-1.45). RTS and ISS did not differ significantly in a formal paired comparison, and neither tool, alone, reliably rules in or out death at realistic trauma prevalence. SI, RTS and ISS should be understood as serving different, complementary roles across the trauma timeline - SI and RTS at the point of acute triage, ISS as a later anatomical benchmark - rather than as competing predictors to be ranked against one another.

articles.title: A 22-Year Retrospective Review of Carolina Jessamine (Gelsemium sempervirens) Plant Exposures Reported to 2 Poison Control Centers.
articles.abstract: IntroductionCarolina jessamine (Gelsemium sempervirens) is an evergreen vine containing highly toxic alkaloids that have caused human injury and death. Because this plant is similar to the honeysuckle plant, foraging errors are common.MethodsRetrospective review of all patients with G. sempervirens ingestions from 1/1/2000 to 4/20/2022 as reported to 2 poison centers that were followed for at least 2 hours post-ingestion. Demographics, clinical effects, intended use of the plant material, whether the plant material was heated, and the presence of case clustering were abstracted. Case outcomes included no effect, minor, moderate, and major effect, with no effect/minor outcomes and moderate/major outcomes grouped for analysis.ResultsThere were 283 cases included, with the majority (n = 266) aged <18 years and a mean age of 7.3 years; the age group with the greatest number of exposures was the 6-to-12-year-old age group (n = 187). There were 57 case clusters in the data set that collectively accounted for 175 of the patients (61.8%). Overall clinical effects were minor, especially in the <6-year-old age group where 100% had no effect/minor outcomes. Cases in which the plant material was heated (n = 11) were more likely to have a severe outcome (27.3%) than those that did not (0.4%); odds ratio 101.6 (95% CI 9.5-1087).ConclusionsOutcomes following pediatric exposure to G. sempervirens were generally mild. Severe illness was more likely in cases where the plant material was heated as part of preparation. Exploratory pediatric exposures to the raw plant material may be observed without HCF referral.

articles.title: Treating the acute, missing the trajectory: the internist's dilemma in older, frail patients.
Comparison of two immobilization techniques for radiological outcomes in fifth metacarpal neck fractures: a prospective controlled study.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Although fifth metacarpal neck fractures are commonly managed conservatively, there is no consensus regarding the optimal immobilization strategy. The aim of this study was to compare the radiographic outcomes of the Jahss Position Splint (JPS) and the conventional Ulnar Gutter Splint (UGS) in the treatment of fifth metacarpal neck fractures. A total of 78 adult male patients treated for isolated closed fifth metacarpal neck fractures between January 2023 and June 2024 were prospectively evaluated. Patients were allocated to either the JPS group (n = 42) or the UGS group (n = 36). Patients were assigned to JPS or UGS according to the predefined odd/even-calendar-day duty schedule of two surgeons, each of whom routinely applied one of the techniques. All patients underwent closed reduction using the Jahss maneuver followed by three weeks of immobilization. Radiographic outcomes included initial fracture angulation (IFA), post-reduction angulation (PRA), final follow-up angulation at 12 weeks (FFA), metacarpal shortening, and malunion rates. No significant differences were observed between the groups regarding age or IFA (p > 0.05). Correction during reduction and splint application was greater with JPS than with UGS (15.2 ± 9.6° vs. 8.9 ± 11.0°; p = 0.009), whereas subsequent loss of reduction during immobilisation did not differ significantly between the groups (2.8 ± 8.4° vs. 1.0 ± 9.8°; p = 0.388).The JPS group demonstrated significantly lower PRA (p < 0.001) and FFA (p = 0.003) compared with the UGS group. Metacarpal shortening was significantly less in the JPS group (p = 0.036). The malunion rate was 5% in the JPS group and 28% in the UGS group (p = 0.009). JPS was associated with greater immediate angular correction and more favourable final radiographic outcomes than UGS but did not reduce subsequent loss of reduction during immobilisation. Because functional and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed, the clinical relevance of these radiographic differences remains uncertain.

articles.title: Surgical management of orbital wall fractures in juveniles: a European multicenter study.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Isolated orbital floor fractures in juveniles are a challenge, as children and adolescents may experience diplopia and limited ocular motility, even with little to no periorbital edema or visible signs of injury to the eye. The aim of the present study is to assess the demographic and clinical variables, and the outcomes of pediatric patients affected by isolated orbital wall fractures at several European oral and maxillofacial surgery centers. Pediatric patients (less than 18 years) with hospitalized and surgically treated for unilateral isolated orbital blow out fractures of the orbital floor and/or the medial wall were included. The following data were recorded for each patient: gender, age, etiology of trauma, site of orbital wall fracture(s), timing of intervention, surgical approach, orbital reconstruction material/implant, post-operative complications RESULTS: A total of 51 pediatric patients (45 boys, 6 girls) with a mean age of 12.1 years were included. Most patients (43 children, 84.3%) presented with an isolated orbital floor fracture. Clinically, the most frequently observed sign was diplopia / double vision (43 patients, 84.3%). More than two thirds (68.6%) of cases were surgically treated within the first two days from injury. In 6 patients (11.8%) one or more persistent postoperative disturbances were found six months postoperatively, including diplopia in 3 subjects (5.9%), infraorbital nerve paresthesia in 2 patients (3.9%), and enophthalmos in 2 patients (3.9%). The rarity of pure orbital wall fractures in pediatric patients makes it difficult to establish uniform evidence-based guidelines for their management. These injuries must also be recognized promptly, as surgical intervention may be required at a very early stage. A reasoned and individualized choice of the optimal surgical approach appears to be the most appropriate strategy for this specific type of facial fracture in the pediatric population. Not applicable.

articles.title: Management and outcomes of moderate-to-severe pelvic ring fractures: a 10-year experience from an Australian Level 1 Trauma Centre.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Moderate-to-severe pelvic ring fractures are associated with high morbidity and mortality despite advances in resuscitation, development in trauma systems and multispecialty haemorrhage control. This study aimed to describe the management strategies and clinical outcomes of moderate-to-severe pelvic ring fractures over a 10-year period at an Australian Level I Trauma Centre. A retrospective observational cohort study was performed of patients aged ≥ 16 years with moderate-to-severe pelvic ring fractures (Abbreviated Injury Scale (AIS) ≥ 3) treated between January 2015 and December 2024. Data were obtained from the institutional prospectively collected trauma registry. A total of 313 patients met the inclusion criteria. The mean age was 47.0 years and 69.3% were male. Motor vehicle (35.1%) and motorcycle collisions (24.9%) accounted for 60.1% of injuries. Median ISS was 26 (IQR 19-34), with 70.6% sustaining pelvic AIS 4-5 injuries. 20.1% of patients underwent at least one haemorrhage-control intervention, including angioembolisation (14.4%), preperitoneal pelvic packing (5.8%) and external fixation (5.8%). Angioembolisation utilisation increased from 6.7% in 2015 to 40.0% in 2024. In-hospital mortality was 7.7%, with traumatic brain injury accounting for 62.5% of deaths and haemorrhagic shock for only one death. Moderate-to-severe pelvic ring fractures remained characterised by high-energy mechanisms and severe multisystem injury over the study period, while management evolved with increasing utilisation of angioembolisation. In-hospital mortality was numerically lower compared with historical cohorts, with most deaths attributable to associated traumatic brain injury rather than pelvic haemorrhage.

articles.title: [Acute heart failure-management during the first 120 min : Approach for early stabilization and decongestion].
articles.abstract: Acute heart failure (AHF) is among the most common causes of emergency department, intermediate care, and intensive care unit admission and remains associated with substantial early mortality despite advances in contemporary therapy. The first 120 min of management are particularly critical, as this period determines not only respiratory and hemodynamic stabilization, but also trigger identification, decongestion strategy, and the foundation for subsequent prognostic improvement. This CME article provides a practical, phenotype-based approach to the early management of AHF. The proposed strategy is centered on the rapid classification of patients according to congestion ("wet" vs. "dry") and perfusion ("warm" vs. "cold") status. Stabilization and diagnostic work-up must occur simultaneously. Early assessment should focus on identifying acute coronary syndrome, clinically relevant arrhythmias, hypertensive crisis, pulmonary embolism, structural heart disease, and infectious triggers. In addition to clinical examination, electrocardiography, blood gas analysis, and biomarkers, point-of-care ultrasound with lung ultrasound and focused echocardiography play a pivotal role in the first-line evaluation. From a therapeutic perspective, early noninvasive ventilation in cardiogenic pulmonary edema, prompt vasodilation in hypertensive presentations, and effective decongestion with intravenous loop diuretics constitute the core interventions. In cases of insufficient response, escalation strategies such as sequential nephron blockade or selective use of vasoactive agents should be considered. Structured reassessment at short intervals is essential to detect persistent congestion, evolving hypoperfusion, inadequate therapeutic response, or overlooked differential diagnoses. The article emphasizes that successful acute management must already establish the transition toward guideline-directed long-term therapy during the first hours of hospitalization, including early initiation of evidence-based heart failure medication once hemodynamic stabilization has been achieved.

articles.title: Prehospital Care of Older Adults Following Perceived Low-Acuity Falls and Related "Lift Assist" Encounters: An NAEMSP Position Statement and Resource Document.
articles.abstract: Older adults who present as low-acuity falls requiring mobilization assistance, commonly referred to as a "lift assist", represent a common reason for EMS activation. These encounters often involve underlying medical conditions or injuries that are not immediately apparent, and missed or delayed diagnosis is associated with adverse outcomes. At the same time, some patients are transported to the emergency department when it is not necessary, exposing them to potential harms and contributing to increased healthcare utilization. These encounters are therefore complex clinical presentations and represent important opportunities for thorough assessment and higher-order clinical decision making, supported by systems that enable appropriate disposition and follow-up. However, there is a system-level bias, beginning in initial education and reinforced through dispatch, policy, and protocol, that frames these encounters as uniformly low-acuity, non-medical, minor traumas leading to underassessment and limiting clinical decision-making. Therefore, NAEMSP recommends:EMS systems should recognize calls for falls or "lift assists" as patient encounters that warrant an assessment, including evaluation for underlying medical causes, traumatic injuries, and safety, and frame these encounters as opportunities for higher-order clinical decision-making within the broader context of geriatric syndromes rather than isolated low-acuity events.EMS systems should support transport decisions based on a thorough assessment and patient-centered discussion, recognizing that not all patients require ED transport and that safe alternatives may include non-transport or referral to appropriate follow-up pathways.EMS systems should track the assessment of patients encountered during "lift assist" responses and older adults following perceived low acuity falls as a system-level quality measure to monitor performance and drive improvement.Policymakers and payers should implement sustainable reimbursement structures that support EMS assessment and care even when transport does not occur.

articles.title: Pediatric Disaster Preparedness at Rural and Critical Access Hospitals: A Mixed-Methods Study.
articles.abstract: Over 80% of pediatric emergency department (ED) visits in the United States occur outside of children's hospitals. Although previous studies have described gaps in pediatric readiness, few studies have focused on pediatric disaster preparedness at rural and critical access hospitals (CAHs). During periods of pediatric surge, CAHs may be forced to manage pediatric patients with delayed transfer times. This mixed-methods study, conducted by the Region V for Kids (RV4K) Pediatric Disaster Center of Excellence, elicited strengths and barriers to pediatric disaster preparedness in rural and CAHs. We conducted a qualitative study of clinicians from CAHs in the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) Region 5. After completing a demographic survey, respondents were invited to participate in focus groups about pediatric disaster preparedness, followed by an open-response questionnaire about how RV4K can support rural and CAHs. Descriptive statistics were calculated. Focus group transcripts and questionnaire responses were analyzed using a constant comparative approach to identify themes. Of the 41 survey respondents, 19 participated in focus groups. Most study participants worked at EDs seeing <1800 children per year, and less than half had pediatric inpatient capabilities. Few hospital disaster plans considered children. Four focus group themes emerged: strengths of staff and community, staffing limitations, and desire for targeted pediatric education resources and pediatric disaster plan development. Our study engaged directly with staff at rural and CAHs to gain insights about pediatric preparedness that will be used to develop resources specifically tailored to CAHs' unique clinical needs.

articles.title: Does End-of-Therapy-Anchored Follow-Up Bias Comparisons of Antibiotic Duration in Acute Otitis Media?
Response to "Prehospital Trauma Compendium: Prehospital Management of Spinal Cord Injuries - A NAEMSP Comprehensive Review and Analysis of the Literature".
Precision Immunosuppression in Heart Transplantation: Biomarker-Guided Therapy Comes of Age.
articles.abstract: Heart transplantation is the definitive treatment for end-stage heart failure. While the number of heart transplant performed yearly in the United States has nearly doubled in the last decade, median survival has stagnated, largely due to the complications posed by lifelong immunosuppression. A shift towards precision medicine is needed to achieve the optimal balance between risk of allograft rejection and drug-related toxicities to improve post-transplant outcomes. Novel molecular based diagnostic tools and biomarkers are being investigated, and hold promise in evaluating graft health and assessing immune state. The use of circulating biomarkers and molecular diagnostics such as human and viral cell-free DNA, tissue-based gene expression profiling, and circulating microRNAs, will allow for more comprehensive assessment of post-transplant immune activity and rejection risk to personalize patient care.
